person.name: Gattu Rithvik
person.line: Third-year IT student in Hyderabad. I build LLM tools and write down what broke.
person.tagline: Curiosity to ideas. Ideas to products.
person.college: B.Tech in Information Technology, Vardhaman College of Engineering

about: I’m a third-year IT student at Vardhaman College of Engineering in Hyderabad, with a 9.2 CGPA. I got into building out of curiosity about how products work, and that led me to AI, independent projects and hackathons.
I work on LLM applications, agents, retrieval and developer tools. I care about what happens after the demo works: whether it’s reliable, useful, and something someone would open twice.

I start with the inconvenience, not the technology: why it exists, who runs into it, whether an idea is feasible. And I write down what broke, because that’s where I learn the most. Every project on the ticket has a line about it.

ticket.title: Projects and experiments
ticket.hint: Scratch the ticket. Each panel is something I built. One is hiding.

projects.title: PromptShield CI
projects.what: A prompt security testing tool. It analyses system prompts, generates adversarial attacks, tests how an LLM application responds, and produces a vulnerability report with suggested fixes.
projects.wrong: Getting the local Mistral model to generate diverse, targeted attacks instead of repetitive or malformed ones was one of the hardest parts. I worked on structured attack categories, retries and validation to make the testing more consistent.

projects.title: POINT.FEEDBACK
projects.what: A visual feedback tool for developers. You point at an element on a webpage, capture context, add comments, and it turns the feedback into a structured development issue.
projects.wrong: The biggest challenge was getting the standalone feedback widget and the backend to talk to each other. Each submission carried screenshots, browser info, DOM details, comments and audio, so getting the multipart request format right took careful debugging.

projects.title: OpsBrain AI
projects.what: An industrial knowledge platform that uses RAG to answer questions from technical and safety documents, show the sources, support compliance audits, and connect lessons from incident records.
projects.wrong: The retrieval pipeline was the hardest part. A fluent answer isn’t necessarily a useful one: chunking, retrieval quality and source relevance matter as much as the model. The demo corpus is only seven documents, so it works end to end but isn’t hardened.

projects.title: Payment Recovery Agent
projects.what: Agent that works out why a subscription payment failed and picks what to do next: retry, offer a discount, send an update link, or escalate to a person.
projects.wrong: A multi-cycle simulation showed over a third of a seeded batch stuck in pending_retry forever. Nothing requeued it, and the retry delays in the config weren’t used anywhere. Fixed, and the delays are real now.

projects.title: Déjà Vu
projects.what: An engineering change-risk tool. It retrieves relevant past engineering experiences, uses them to assess a proposed change, and answers SHIP, REVIEW or HOLD. It accounts for earlier overrides and marks outdated lessons stale.
projects.wrong: Making Hindsight memory return experiences that actually changed the decision was the hard part. Memory in an agent isn’t enough if the retrieved context doesn’t influence the call. Also, the 65% drop in wrong calls comes from a simulated benchmark with a scripted oracle. It shows the mechanism, not real-world accuracy.

projects.title: Ripple
projects.what: A lightweight Python CLI that analyses Git history to find files that often change together, then checks your staged changes for related files you may have missed.
projects.wrong: Finding meaningful co-change patterns without treating every historical correlation as a dependency was the interesting challenge. I benchmarked it on the newest 100 commits of three small Python repos, which is a small sample, and it taught me to think about confidence and the difference between a useful warning and a misleading one.

projects.title: ClausePilot
projects.event: Hack2skill: AI for Legal Assistance and Access
projects.what: Reads a freelance contract, compares each clause with standard ones, flags the risky ones, and drafts counter-messages plus a prep sheet for talking to a lawyer.
projects.wrong: The live demo ran through a Cloudflare tunnel from my laptop. Fine for a demo, not a deployment.

projects.title: FlowSync, the one I shelved
projects.what: Started as a Hyderabad traffic-routing demo. I turned it into an energy-corridor risk tool: live news signals, a scenario modeller for refinery run-rates and fuel prices, and a ranking engine for procurement options.
projects.wrong: I built two projects for the same hackathon and had to pick one. OpsBrain went forward, FlowSync didn’t. Along the way the Gemini key went invalid so I switched to Groq, Google Maps billing blocked me so I hardcoded the corridors, and Cloudflare returned a 403 on my Python requests until I switched to httpx. A route screen from the old traffic app also had to go, because point-to-point routing makes no sense for shipping corridors.
